title: Does Organic Farming Grow Less Food?

scenes.purpose: Pose the first question as a picture the viewer can hold: two fields at harvest.

visual.description: The question types on, large and centred, as it is spoken; 'come up short' turns amber.
onScreenText: Does the organic field come up short?

scenes.direction: Cold open; beat after the question mark.
scenes.narration: Picture two fields growing the same crop, one farmed organically and one not. At harvest, does the organic field come up short, and by how much?

scenes.purpose: Show the two confident, opposite answers side by side.

visual.description: Split field: left half reads 'organic grows less', right half 'organic grows just as much', each appearing as the narration says it.

scenes.direction: Left half on 'grows less', right half on 'just as much'.
scenes.narration: Ask around and you hear both answers with total confidence: organic grows less, or organic grows just as much.

scenes.purpose: Set up the second question the video will answer.

visual.description: The second question types on; 'greener' turns green-amber and holds.
onScreenText: Is it still the greener choice?

scenes.direction: Type on with the narration; hold a beat before the first question section.
scenes.narration: And the answer sets up a second question: if organic does grow less, is it still the greener choice?

scenes.purpose: The claim that organic grows less, in the creator's own words.

visual.description: Quote card: the words appear as spoken; '25% lower' turns amber.
onScreenText: "organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: AsapSCIENCE told its viewers that "organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones".

scenes.purpose: The opposite claim, then the question that turns to the data.

visual.description: Quote card: the words appear as spoken; 'as much food or more' turns amber; the card dims on 'So who is right?'.
onScreenText: "you can grow as much food or more food better food without all those chemicals"

scenes.direction: Dim the card on s06; beat before the data.
scenes.narration: Mark Hyman says the opposite: "you can grow as much food or more food better food without all those chemicals". So who is right?

scenes.purpose: The pooled yield gap and its range.

visual.description: Three tiles: the central 19.2% lands first and largest, then the 15.5% and 22.9% ends of the range flank it as the range is spoken.

chart.title: Organic yields vs conventional, pooled comparisons
chart.note: An average over many systems and crops; the authors say it may still be an overestimate.

scenes.direction: Centre tile on '19.2%', flanking tiles on the range; hold through the caveat.
scenes.narration: A meta-analysis by Lauren Ponisio and colleagues pooled side-by-side yield comparisons and found organic yields 19.2% lower than conventional, with a likely range of 15.5 to 22.9%, and the authors warn that even this may overstate the gap, because the published studies lean towards reporting bigger conventional wins.

scenes.purpose: Show the paper's own words: conventional ahead for every crop type, and a smaller gap than before.

visual.description: The results paragraph; 'significantly higher than organic for all crop types' highlights on s08.

excerpt.highlight: Conventional yields were significantly higher than organic for all crop types

scenes.direction: Highlight sweeps on s08; hold through s09.
scenes.narration: Conventional came out ahead for every crop type the study grouped, and for most of those types the gap was about the same size. That gap is real, but it is smaller than the ones earlier meta-analyses had reported.

scenes.purpose: The mechanism: nitrogen limits organic yields.

visual.description: The fertilisation paragraph of the review; the nitrogen sentence highlights as it is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: Typically, crop yield is limited by plant N availability in organic but not in conventional systems

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'nitrogen'.
scenes.narration: Why lower at all? A review of organic food and health, citing earlier work, points to fertiliser: in organic systems crop yield is typically limited by how much nitrogen the plants can get, which is not the case in conventional systems.

scenes.purpose: The dissenting report, and how thin its yield statement is.

visual.description: The AAP abstract lines; 'yields comparable to those' highlights on s11, then the rest of the abstract dims on s12 to show it is one sentence.

scenes.direction: Highlight on s11; hold on s12; beat before the answer.
scenes.narration: Not everyone agrees: a clinical report for pediatricians says well-designed farming studies show organic yields comparable to conventional farming. But in the report's summary, the part we could read, that is one sentence, with no yield figure and no studies named.

scenes.purpose: The answer: about a fifth less on average, much less with rotations and mixtures.

visual.description: Three horizontal bars: the pooled 19.2% gap first, then the shorter multi-cropping and crop-rotation gaps grow in as 'rotated or grown in mixtures' is spoken.

chart.title: Organic yield gap
chart.note: Gap is organic yield below conventional; the diversified subsets are not the whole dataset.

scenes.direction: First bar on 'a fifth'; the two shorter bars on 'rotated or grown in mixtures'.
scenes.narration: So on the pooled data, yes: organic fields grew less, by roughly a fifth or perhaps a little less, but where crops were rotated or grown in mixtures the gap shrank to about 8 or 9%.

scenes.purpose: Turn to the second question.

visual.description: The question types on; 'more land' turns amber.
onScreenText: Does organic need more land for the same food?

scenes.direction: Type on with the narration; beat after.
scenes.narration: Which raises the next question: if each organic field grows less, does organic need more land for the same food, and does that undo its green reputation?

scenes.purpose: The green reputation, stated plainly.

visual.description: Quote card: the words appear as spoken; 'healthier for the planet' turns amber.
onScreenText: "Organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: Harvard Health put it plainly: "Organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet".

scenes.purpose: The pediatric report agrees.

visual.description: Quote card: the words appear as spoken; 'less environmental impact' turns amber.
onScreenText: "has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches"

scenes.direction: Card replaces the previous one.
scenes.narration: The same pediatric report agrees, saying organic farming "has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches".

scenes.purpose: Name the change of yardstick before the numbers.

visual.description: One line: 'per unit of food, not per field'; 'per unit of food' turns amber.
onScreenText: per unit of food, not per field

scenes.direction: Line lands on 'per unit of food'.
scenes.narration: But a meta-analysis by Clark and Tilman measured the impacts per unit of food, not per field, using studies that assessed both systems within the same publication.

scenes.purpose: The per-food scorecard: more land, less energy, more nutrient pollution, similar emissions, at a local scale.

visual.description: Four tiles, one per indicator, each landing as it is spoken: land 25% to 110% more, energy 15% less, eutrophication 37% higher, greenhouse gas 4% lower (not significant). On s21 the tiles dim slightly to mark the local-scale caveat.

chart.title: Organic vs conventional, per unit of food
chart.note: Within-publication comparisons at a local scale; the greenhouse gas difference was not significant.

scenes.direction: One tile per indicator as narrated; dim on s21.
scenes.narration: Measured that way, organic systems needed 25 to 110% more land. They used 15% less energy, but had 37% higher eutrophication potential, a measure of nutrient pollution. Greenhouse gas emissions came out similar, because relying on manure turns more of a farm's nitrogen into nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. The authors add that these are comparisons at a local scale, and the picture might differ regionally, nationally or globally.

scenes.purpose: The authors' own warning against reading this as a win for conventional.

visual.description: The discussion paragraph; 'this should not be taken as an' highlights as the warning is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: this should not be taken as an

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'warn against'.
scenes.narration: And they warn against reading this as a win for conventional farming, which uses more energy and relies on high fertiliser, herbicide and pesticide inputs that can harm health and the environment.

scenes.purpose: What actually dwarfs the organic question: the food itself.

visual.description: One line lands large: '20 to 100 times'; 'times' holds in amber.
onScreenText: 20 to 100 times the impacts of plant-based foods

citations.label: Clark and Tilman 2017, ruminant meats vs plant-based foods

scenes.direction: Camera punch on '20 to 100 times'; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: What does dwarf the organic question is the food itself: on every indicator they examined, ruminant meats had 20 to 100 times the impacts of plant-based foods, a difference far larger than the one between farming systems.

scenes.purpose: The answer to the second question.

visual.description: One line: 'not clearly greener'; it lands as spoken and holds.

scenes.direction: Line lands on 'not clearly greener'; beat before the close.
scenes.narration: So per unit of food, organic is not clearly greener: it trades lower energy use for more land and more nutrient pollution, with emissions about even.

scenes.purpose: The first habit to take away.

visual.description: The question types on; 'how many' turns amber.

scenes.direction: Type on with the narration.
scenes.narration: The next time a label or a video says organic grows just as much, ask which studies, and how many.

scenes.purpose: The second habit, and the closing line.

visual.description: The question types on; 'per what' turns amber and holds to the end.

scenes.direction: Type on; hold to fade out.
scenes.narration: And when something is sold as better for the planet, ask: better per what? Per plate of food, the answer here was mixed.
